1.pericope_label: Plucking the ears of corn: the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the meaning of the double-numbered sabbath largely conjectural, lists six proposals without choosing, and prefers the one that would explain how so peculiar a term arose; Barnes follows Scaliger to the first sabbath after the second day of unleavened bread; Robertson cuts the knot, calling the reading undoubtedly spurious and reconstructing the scribal accident that produced it, since if it were genuine we should not know what it means.
Calvin makes the day the second of the great annual sabbaths; Gill canvasses four theories before preferring much the same result.

Clarke concludes with Lightfoot for the first sabbath after the second day of unleavened bread, adds the practical argument that no Jew might eat green ears before then nor find any standing after Pentecost, reports the manuscripts and versions that omit the word, and preserves the saying about the man working on the sabbath that one old copy inserts here.
Henry declines the enquiry outright, blessed be God we need not be critical in this matter, and takes from David's example that ceremonial appointments may be dispensed with in cases of necessity.
Theophylact makes Christ speak as legislator, Lord of the sabbath because he ordained it and therefore able to loose it.
Cyril of Alexandria answers the objectors in the second person, asking whether they do not themselves break bread when they set out their own sabbath meal.

Tertullian argues against Marcion that in interfering with the sabbath Christ acted after the Creator's own example, the ark having been carried round Jericho for eight days running and so on a sabbath.

positions.view: a real day in the calendar, variously identified
the reading is spurious and means nothing
the question need not be pressed at all

outliers.claim: the sabbath was interfered with after the Creator's own example, since the ark was carried round Jericho for eight days running

themes: And it came to pass on the second sabbath after the first, that he went through the corn fields; and his disciples plucked the ears of corn, and did eat, rubbing them in their hands.
And certain of the Pharisees said unto them, Why do ye that which is not lawful to do on the sabbath days?
And Jesus answering them said, Have ye not read so much as this, what David did, when himself was an hungred, and they which were with him;
How he went into the house of God, and did take and eat the shewbread, and gave also to them that were with him; which it is not lawful to eat but for the priests alone?
And he said unto them, That the Son of man is Lord also of the sabbath.

6.pericope_label: The man whose right hand was withered: is it lawful on the sabbath to do good?

schools.summary: Robertson claims the specified right hand and the double compound verb for the physician's eye and wonders whether Luke alone notes the day from professional experience; Ellicott finds this narrative and Mark's agreeing more closely with each other than either does with Matthew; Barnes lists four causes of the fury that followed.
Calvin lets both reports stand without a sequence, since the Pharisees may have spoken plainly and Christ still have discerned the design behind their words.

Clarke prosecutes a running quarrel with a rationalising critic who made the withered hand a dislocated arm, first refusing refutation and four verses later granting the premise to answer it, and closes with the question why all this learned labour to leave God out.
Henry draws the moral that Christ was neither ashamed nor afraid to own the purposes of his grace though he knew his enemies would take advantage of it.
Cyril of Alexandria supplies the envious man's motive, that he makes the praises of others food for his own disease, and suggests the man was set in the midst to shame the unpitying into compassion.

Bede states the dilemma the watchers set, cruelty if he did not heal and sabbath-breaking if he did; Augustine reconciles the two reports in sequence, the Pharisees asking first and Christ, perceiving they wanted a charge, setting the man in the midst and asking in turn.

debates.question: Who put the question about healing on the sabbath, and in what order?

positions.view: the Pharisees asked first and Christ answered by asking in turn
no sequence is needed; Luke records only that Christ saw through a design the words did not express

outliers.claim: Luke's omission of the Herodians may be due to his own acquaintance with people connected with the Herods, which made him reluctant to give them prominence

themes: And it came to pass also on another sabbath, that he entered into the synagogue and taught: and there was a man whose right hand was withered.
And the scribes and Pharisees watched him, whether he would heal on the sabbath day; that they might find an accusation against him.
But he knew their thoughts, and said to the man which had the withered hand, Rise up, and stand forth in the midst. And he arose and stood forth.
Then said Jesus unto them, I will ask you one thing; Is it lawful on the sabbath days to do good, or to do evil? to save life, or to destroy it?
And looking round about upon them all, he said unto the man, Stretch forth thy hand. And he did so: and his hand was restored whole as the other.
And they were filled with madness; and communed one with another what they might do to Jesus.

12.pericope_label: He continued all night in prayer, and chose twelve, whom also he named apostles

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the phrase as the oratory of God, a place of prayer by running water, and gathers instances from Philippi to Tiberias, while admitting that a precisely harmonised arrangement of the choosing seems impossible and calling the difficulty happily unimportant; Robertson denies that sense flatly and insists on the actual night-long prayer of Jesus, noting the verb for passing the whole night occurs only here; Lightfoot brings the rabbinic tradition that God himself prays by authority and confesses he cannot but laugh at their triflings.
Clarke lists three things that unite in a genuine apostle: knowledge of God himself, commission from the Head of the Church, and preaching accompanied by the Spirit.

Henry decides against the oratory because Christ sought privacy, makes the night an example of secret prayer against our half-hours in the closet, and notes that the order of the twelve differs in each of the three lists.
Cyril draws the lesson of going apart in secret with worldly cares laid aside, the mind raised to divine contemplation.

Ambrose finds the significance in who was passed over, fishermen and publicans rather than the wise, the rich or the noble, so that the force of truth rather than the graces of oratory might prevail; Augustine allows a man two or three names and presses that Judas was chosen knowingly, Christ refusing not even this share of human infirmity.

debates.question: Does the phrase mean prayer to God or a house of prayer?

positions.view: a place set apart for prayer, the oratory of God
the actual prayer of Jesus to the Father, all night long
declines to say whether the rabbinic sense applies here

outliers.claim: Christ was willing to be betrayed by his own apostle so that a man betrayed by his friend might bear calmly his mistaken judgment and his kindness thrown away

themes: And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God.
And when it was day, he called unto him his disciples: and of them he chose twelve, whom also he named apostles;
Simon, (whom he also named Peter,) and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew,
Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alpheus, and Simon called Zelotes,
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.

17.pericope_label: The whole multitude sought to touch him: virtue went out of him, and healed them all

schools.summary: Barnes gives three reasons for identity with the other sermon and answers the objections by observing that only the healing is placed on the plain; Robertson denies there is the slightest reason for putting one sermon on the mountain and the other in the valley, and defends the reports against the charge of being assembled from isolated sayings; Ellicott is least willing to settle it, since events these two place before the choice are placed by Matthew after the mission.
Clarke agrees with the identification and calls the whole sequence striking, the ascent, the night of prayer, the separating of the twelve, the descent, and the healing of the diseased in the plain.

Cyril of Alexandria stresses that the election was not made in a corner but before a vast concourse that included idolaters from the sea coast, teachers appointed in sight of all; and he reads the outgoing power as proof that Christ borrowed strength from no one but healed by the putting forth of his own.

Ambrose finds the antithesis in the movement, Christ ascending with the apostles and descending to the multitude, since the crowd neither follows him to the heights nor climbs them, and in high places there are no sick.

debates.question: Is this discourse the Sermon on the Mount?

positions.view: yes, one discourse; the level place lies on the mountain side
the resemblances are many, but the order of events resists harmonising

outliers.claim: a preacher who is no vehicle of power from Christ may well ask himself why

themes: And he came down with them, and stood in the plain, and the company of his disciples, and a great multitude of people out of all Judea and Jerusalem, and from the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon, which came to hear him, and to be healed of their diseases;
And they that were vexed with unclean spirits: and they were healed.
And the whole multitude sought to touch him: for there went virtue out of him, and healed them all.

20.pericope_label: Blessed be ye poor: but woe unto you that are rich, for ye have received your consolation

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the missing words decisive for two separate occasions, corrects blessed be to blessed are and the kingdom to God's, and hears pity rather than denunciation in the woes; Barnes fills in the psychology of the rich, too proud to ask and too satisfied to want; Robertson notes the lifted eyes peculiar to this opening.
Calvin finds four blessings answered by four curses and restricts the curse to those so occupied with possessions that they forget the life to come.

Basil cautions that nothing involuntary deserves a blessing, since all virtue is characterised by freedom of the will, and that many are poor in possessions and most covetous in disposition; Chrysostom expounds godly sorrow and ends that we often find the Lord sorrowing, never laughing.
Cyril of Alexandria harmonises instead, holding that the evangelists do not contradict but divide the narrative between them and often recapitulate, and distinguishes the two senses of poor.
Tertullian turns the woe against Marcion, since a god who condescends to curse proves himself capable of anger and is no impassible deity.

debates.question: Are these beatitudes the same discourse as the other report?

positions.view: no; dropping in spirit would be too great a difficulty, so the occasions differ
yes; the evangelists divide one narrative between them and recapitulate

outliers.claim: pronouncing a woe is evidence that the speaker is capable of offence and anger, and so not the impassible deity Marcion describes

themes: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said, Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God.
Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh.
Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you from their company, and shall reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man’s sake.
Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy: for, behold, your reward is great in heaven: for in the like manner did their fathers unto the prophets.
But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation.
Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep.
Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets.

27.pericope_label: Love your enemies: as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise

schools.summary: Robertson puts the weight on the contrastive particle, calls the blow violence rather than contempt, and admits the difficulty that Jesus himself protested when struck; Ellicott observes that this report inverts the garments and points to direct violence where the other points to legal process, and ends the section by arguing from the different arrangement of the precepts against the identity of the two discourses.

Gill restricts the hearers to those who had received the traditions of the elders, which the rules that follow oppose; Calvin denies the clause concerns a request for assistance at all, referring it to actions at law, and guards it so that a good man may still recover his own by lawful means.

Wesley reads a change of audience from particular sorts of persons to all in general, and treats the cheek and the cloak as proverbial for an invasion of the tenderest points of honour and property; Clarke distinguishes the garments after Bishop Pearce and refers the clause about asking back to extortion by tax-gatherers and soldiers.

Henry takes the address widely, to all that hear and not to disciples only, states the golden rule as putting our souls into their souls' stead, and following Hammond reads the goods as borrowed rather than stolen.

Chrysostom compares the persecutor to a madman attacking his physician and argues that the golden rule lies within nature, Christ having ordained nothing beyond what was long before implanted in the conscience; Basil turns the command on the powerful, for whom readiness to take revenge is a great dishonour.
Cyril reads the passage as a schooling in contempt of property, the merciful man conferring on his persecutors the benefits by which he assists his friends.
Bede marks the hinge, from what they might suffer at their enemies' hands to how they ought to behave towards them.

debates.question: What does the clause about not asking back forbid?

positions.view: actions at law by which bad men carry off the property of others
begging off goods seized by extortion, which should be borne quietly
demanding repayment from an insolvent borrower

outliers.claim: the prohibition means do not hinder him in his robbing, though it is usually useless anyhow with modern armed bandits

themes: But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you,
Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.
And unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the other; and him that taketh away thy cloke forbid not to take thy coat also.
Give to every man that asketh of thee; and of him that taketh away thy goods ask them not again.
And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.

32.pericope_label: Lend, hoping for nothing again: be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful

schools.summary: Ellicott refers the wider term to the writer's Gentile audience and distinguishes what thank from what reward; Robertson blames the Latin rendering for centuries of European prohibition of interest and defends never despairing of repayment as the sense.
Calvin denies the application to usury altogether, since the preceding verses have a wider reference and Christ exhorts only to duties performed freely.

Clarke takes the word for heathens, where the other report has tax-gatherers, and warns against a life containing nothing that a Turk's would not; Wesley presses that the returning of love for love does not even deserve thanks, since a man may do it who has not taken a step in Christianity.

Chrysostom explains that nothing earthly engenders spiritual love, which is not even overcome of malice; Gregory of Nyssa says a man will not err who calls the harsh calculation of interest theft or homicide; Basil elaborates the breeding metaphor latent in the Greek name for interest and turns the precept into God's own suretyship for the poor.
Cyril closes on mercy as the virtue that makes us like to God and imprints on the soul signs of a heavenly nature.
Tertullian reads the older prohibitions of usury as a graduated preparation for the gospel, the law first eradicating the fruit of the money lent to accustom a man to losing the money itself.

debates.question: Is lend, hoping for nothing again a prohibition of usury?

positions.view: yes; interest is theft, and the older law forbade it by stages
no; it is a mistake to confine the statement to usury
the received rendering is wrong; the sense is never despairing of repayment

outliers.claim: the Latin rendering hoping for nothing thence drove money-lending into Jewish hands and added greatly to the detestation in which Jews were held

themes: For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them.
And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same.
And if ye lend to them of whom ye hope to receive, what thank have ye? for sinners also lend to sinners, to receive as much again.

But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.
Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.

37.pericope_label: Judge not: cast out first the beam out of thine own eye

schools.summary: Ellicott finds a climax in the three prohibitions and reads the third as release or acquittal, a quasi-judicial act rather than the forgiveness of a private wrong; Robertson takes the present imperatives as forbidding the habit of criticism rather than the forming of opinions; Lightfoot supplies the temple's heaped and struck measures; Barnes takes the saying about the disciple of attainment, blind guides breeding blind followers.

Calvin presses that concession much further, since the children of God frequently receive the very worst reward, and adds that believers provoke severity by their own excessive severity; Gill holds these sayings were gathered rather than spoken at one time.
Clarke illustrates the bosom from Herodotus' story of Alcmaeon loading himself with Croesus' gold, and notes that the closing maxim already stood in the Jerusalem Targum, a rule the hearers allowed.
Henry states the reciprocity flatly, with Adoni-bezek for a warning, while conceding that providence does not always go by this rule.
Theophylact answers how a running-over return can still be the same measure, since the promise says the same measure and not just as great a one.
Cyril traces judging to its root, that men look into the things of others and forget their own passions.

debates.question: Does the promise of like treatment hold in this life?

positions.view: ordinarily yes, though the exact retributions are reserved for another world
frequently not; promises relating to the present life are not without exceptions

outliers.claim: the connection of thought at the disciple is not above his master is obscure, and some links may have been omitted

themes: Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven:

Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.
And he spake a parable unto them, Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch?
The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master.
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?

Either how canst thou say to thy brother, Brother, let me pull out the mote that is in thine eye, when thou thyself beholdest not the beam that is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, cast out first the beam out of thine own eye, and then shalt thou see clearly to pull out the mote that is in thy brother’s eye.

43.pericope_label: The tree is known by his own fruit: he digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock

schools.summary: Ellicott compares the differing pairings of thorns, figs and thistles, notes the bramble is the Greek Old Testament's word for the burning bush, and reports that the better copies read because it had been well built; Robertson makes the digging down to rock the whole point and notes that the word for the ruin is a medical term for a laceration.

Gill notes that in the other report the saying is aimed at false teachers where here it falls on men busy censuring their brethren; Calvin narrows the test to doctrine and answers the objection that the worst hearts are often the best speakers.
Clarke has the tongue for a pump that empties the heart but neither fills nor cleanses it, and closes with a rigid predestinarian's warning against the Calvinian assurance of predestination.
Chrysostom states the logic, that the tree causes the fruit but the fruit is what gives us knowledge of the tree.

Isidore of Pelusium guards the figure from fatalism, since what is excluded is continuance in evil and not repentance, and asks how a corrupt heart shall bring forth good fruit; Cyril sees the treasure of the heart as the same doctrine set out under another figure.

Bede keeps the tree against the hypocrites, works making up what words set forth; Ambrose allegorises the grape that rots near the ground and ripens on the higher branches, none escaping the condemnation of the flesh but he whom Christ redeemed; Augustine uses the shared ending to argue that the mountain and the plain are one occasion, Christ descending from the summit to level ground on the mountain side.

debates.question: What does the tree and its fruit test?

positions.view: the doctrine of those who profess to be servants of God
the censurer who condemns his brother while his own fruit is corrupt

outliers.claim: neither astrological speculation nor the Calvinian assurance of predestination shows a man his eternal state; only examination of the heart and of the life does

themes: For a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit; neither doth a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.
For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes.

A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.
And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?
Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, and doeth them, I will shew you to whom he is like:

He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock.

But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great.
